profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the Applied ML workstream and the Developer Productivity workstream at a mid-sized SaaS company preparing an internal pilot of a 'team mood from chat' dashboard for engineering managers. The ML side has a sentence-level classifier that labels chat messages as positive, neutral, or negative from Slack and Zulip exports, while Developer Productivity owns the warehouse ingestion, weekly dashboard refresh, and manager-facing rollout. The meeting happens ten days before the pilot review and is meant to align on the Friday handoff, the exact warehouse export to score, the definition of 'ready' on the shared launch checklist, and what Wednesday's staging validation should prove. The agenda is to confirm the weekly mood report contents, verify which engineering chat export the scoring job will consume, walk through the launch checklist item called 'handoff ready,' and confirm the staging run before dashboard wiring. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on the deliverable due Friday, the checklist status for next week, and the staging validation plan for the shared pipeline.

members.name: Nina Park
members.expertise: NLP pipelines, sentiment classification, model packaging, offline evaluation, batch inference
members.background: Nina previously shipped internal text analytics services at a startup and now owns the classifier and feature-generation layer for internal engineering analytics tools.
members.private_state: She wants to freeze the interface this week so she can focus on calibration and threshold tuning instead of integration churn, and she is quietly trying to keep the pilot framed as coarse-grained trend analysis rather than something managers can interrogate message by message.
hidden_assumptions: A 'weekly mood report' is the compact aggregate feed consumed by the dashboard layer, not an explorable report with evidence rows.

When people say 'the warehouse export,' they mean the compliance-approved engineering_chat_curated export that already excludes DMs and channels without the engineering-public or reviewed-project tag.
The launch checklist item 'handoff ready' is satisfied once the output schema, partitioning, and batch job are stable enough for another team to integrate against without surprises.
A Wednesday 'staging run' is mainly about validating contract compatibility and recent-data behavior on a safe snapshot, not proving full production operations end to end.
If someone wants representative examples behind a score, that would come from a later analysis workflow, not from the first pilot deliverable.

members.name: Omar Velasquez
members.expertise: Engineering analytics, internal dashboards, data platform coordination, manager-facing operational rollouts
members.background: Omar came from an enterprise observability team and now coordinates tools that combine repo, ticket, and communication signals into a unified engineering health view.
members.private_state: He needs the pilot to look operationally complete to engineering managers and wants to avoid a launch where his team has to explain missing slices, manual refresh steps, or numbers that cannot be traced back when challenged.
hidden_assumptions: A 'weekly mood report' should be something a manager can inspect enough to understand why a team's score moved, even if only through sampled examples or drill-down slices.

When people say 'the warehouse export,' they mean the standard engineering_chat export used by dashboards, which includes all engineering-tagged Slack and mirrored project channels unless explicitly filtered out downstream.
The checklist item 'handoff ready' means the feature can be put on the normal weekly refresh schedule with no handholding from the producing team.
A Wednesday 'staging run' should demonstrate that the pipeline behaves correctly on a current snapshot close enough to production freshness that Monday's scheduled refresh is de-risked.
If the dashboard shows a trend number to managers, the underlying feed should already support at least light trust-building inspection, not just opaque aggregates.

misalignment_points.topic: What the weekly mood report contains
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to deliver the 'weekly mood report' on Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a dashboard-ingestion artifact: one weekly table with team, channel, positive/neutral/negative percentages, message counts, and week-over-week deltas.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a manager-consumable report surface: the weekly aggregates plus enough drill-down or sampled evidence rows for a manager to sanity-check a movement in score.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In internal analytics work, 'report' naturally refers either to a machine-consumable summary feed or to a human-facing explorable output, and each person's interpretation fits the same rollout conversation well enough that neither hears a contradiction.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the model will run on 'the warehouse export' or 'the engineering chat export.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the curated table engineering_chat_curated.v2, a reviewed export used in prior evaluation that filters to public engineering Slack channels and a small set of approved mirrored project streams in Zulip.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the broader dashboard source table engineering_chat_export_current, the standard warehouse dump for engineering analytics that includes all engineering-tagged channels and mirrored private project channels available under compliance controls.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both tables are widely referred to informally as 'the warehouse export' inside the company because they originate from the same ingestion pipeline and share most columns; since neither person experiences this as introducing a new dataset, the reference feels settled rather than worth naming precisely.

misalignment_points.topic: What the checklist item 'handoff ready' means
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the launch checklist should show the model package as 'handoff ready' next week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'handoff ready' means the producing team can freeze the schema, publish a stable partitioned scoring table, and hand over an artifact that downstream engineers can integrate against without further ML-side changes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'handoff ready' means the feature can sit on the normal Monday refresh path, populate the dashboard automatically, and require no manual intervention or special coordination after launch.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both meanings are plausible interpretations of the same checklist phrase, the conversation can proceed through shared language about 'readiness' and 'handoff' while each person silently fills in a different acceptance bar from their own workstream's definition of done.

misalignment_points.topic: What Wednesday's staging run is validating
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to 'run it in staging on Wednesday against a recent export.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 plans to score a recent but fixed snapshot from the prior completed week in staging, because 'recent export' means up-to-date schema and representative data shape without relying on in-flight late-arriving messages.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 plans to validate against the latest near-current warehouse snapshot available Wednesday morning, because 'recent export' means freshness close enough to production that the scheduled Monday refresh behavior is meaningfully tested.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both approaches are standard and both can honestly be described as using 'a recent export in staging'; the difference is only in freshness expectations, which is exactly the sort of second-order operational detail teams usually leave implicit when they think the environment and dataset family are already agreed.
